recent_posts.title: DOC • Collected consciousness
recent_posts.summary: A deep exploration of why generative AI cannot replace human creativity, arguing that AI models are fundamentally pattern-visualization machines that produce content without meaning, intention, or truth. The author draws on Picasso's Guernica to illustrate how human art carries context and intent that AI cannot replicate. Rather than dismissing AI entirely, the piece proposes a framework for designing AI as a creative collaborator using three roles: Puller (gathering context), Pusher (suggesting directions), and Producer (generating artifacts). A practical workshop case study demonstrates how this framework can be applied to help designers create documentation more efficiently, keeping humans in creative control while AI handles tedious or generative support tasks.

recent_posts.title: DOC • Perspective
recent_posts.summary: A philosophical essay on what it means to have a professional perspective in design. Perspective is defined as a structured, rational argument—not a personal preference—that guides decisions about what to include and exclude in a product. The piece argues that true perspective is an active choice, not a passive skill, and that designers must be able to justify decisions based on user and business goals rather than aesthetics. It warns against committee-driven design that seeks consensus at the cost of conviction, and positions perspective as the key differentiator for human designers in an era of generative AI, which tends toward the statistical average. Examples from Virgin America, Snapchat, Dyson, and Semafor illustrate how bold, singular stances create memorable and disruptive products.

recent_posts.title: Why designers losing influence is a technical literacy problem not an AI problem
recent_posts.summary: AI tools like Figma AI and Figma Sites haven't created a crisis in design — they've exposed a decade-long erosion of technical literacy among designers. The industry collectively decided designers don't need to code, producing professionals who can't evaluate AI-generated output, spot accessibility violations, or participate meaningfully in technical trade-off discussions. Evidence includes 210 WCAG violations in Figma's own demo sites, Builder.ai's collapse after faking AI with 700 engineers, and a 50% drop in entry-level design hiring at Big Tech. The argument isn't that designers must write production code, but that strategic literacy — understanding APIs, performance constraints, data models, and technical debt — is now the baseline for maintaining influence in product decisions increasingly driven by technical considerations.

recent_posts.title: DOC • A new navigation paradigm
recent_posts.summary: AI doesn't eliminate navigation in digital products—it delegates it to invisible algorithmic systems. This shift transforms users from active navigators into passive recipients, potentially causing cognitive debt through the loss of formative practices like searching, comparing, and organizing information. Drawing on Bernard Stiegler's concept of pharmakon, the essay argues that technology is simultaneously remedy and poison, requiring a therapeutic approach to design that restores navigation's formative value while mitigating the risks of cognitive atrophy and algorithmic opacity.

recent_posts.title: DOC • Critique
recent_posts.summary: Design critiques are structured sessions that pressure-test assumptions through constructive friction, not personal taste or governance checkpoints. They help designers build organizational capital by forcing them to articulate business value and defend decisions under friendly scrutiny. Effective critiques require proper facilitation, strategic vulnerability in showing unfinished work, and focus on high-leverage questions rather than tactical details. The practice becomes increasingly valuable as AI accelerates design production, since human judgment is needed to stress-test ideas with contextual knowledge and vision. Critiques develop critical thinking skills and help teams establish shared definitions of quality.

recent_posts.title: Why AI systems need to forget like humans do
recent_posts.summary: Infinite memory in AI systems like ChatGPT may hinder human growth by reinforcing past behaviors and preferences, similar to social media filter bubbles. Human forgetting is an evolutionary feature that enables adaptation and imagination, not a flaw. The article explores how memory-equipped LLMs risk trapping users in outdated versions of themselves and proposes solutions including user-controlled memory management interfaces, time-aware memory systems, and adaptive forgetting mechanisms inspired by neuroscience. Developers and designers must intentionally build forgetting capabilities into AI systems to support user evolution rather than stagnation.

recent_posts.title: DOC • The UX butterfly effect
recent_posts.summary: Design decisions create ripple effects that extend far beyond their immediate purpose, often leading to unintended consequences. Using social media platforms like TikTok as a case study, this piece demonstrates how reinforcing feedback loops can generate both societal impacts (mental health issues, reduced study time) and environmental costs (massive CO₂ emissions from data centers). Systems maps, impact ripple canvases, and iceberg visuals are introduced as practical tools to identify and plan for these hidden consequences by revealing the invisible components—culture, values, beliefs—that drive unexpected outcomes. Organizations that ignore broader systemic impacts face regulatory penalties, while those that map their systems can better understand their role in society and innovate more responsibly.

recent_posts.title: DOC • Interface
recent_posts.summary: Interfaces serve as bridges that translate human intent into action, evolving from command lines to GUIs to modern AI-powered systems. The rise of Large Language Models and generative UI is transforming interface design from static screens to dynamic, personalized experiences that adapt in real-time. Future interfaces will be omnimodal, combining multiple interaction methods simultaneously, while designers shift from architects to choreographers who define flexible frameworks rather than fixed layouts. Despite technological advances toward "no interface" solutions like brain-computer interfaces, the visual and expressive aspects of interfaces remain crucial for human connection and self-expression.

recent_posts.title: DOC • The creator and the machine
recent_posts.summary: Explores the historical relationship between creativity and computational tools, tracing computer art from 1950s pioneers like Georg Nees and Vera Molnár to modern AI-assisted design. The piece examines how artists have long shared authorship with machines, discusses the shift from direct creation to abstraction-based processes, and addresses the ongoing debate about creative ownership in an age of generative AI. It emphasizes that human-machine collaboration in creativity isn't new but has intensified, requiring designers to become orchestrators rather than direct executors of their ideas.

recent_posts.title: How metaphors transform our understanding of complex technology
recent_posts.summary: Metaphors bridge the unfamiliar with the familiar by connecting abstract concepts to human-scale experiences. The evolution of brain metaphors reflects each era's dominant technology, from hydraulic systems to computer networks. In computing, the paper metaphor revolutionized interfaces by making complex machines accessible through familiar office concepts like desktops, folders, and trash cans. Smartphones later adopted physics-based interactions like pinch-to-zoom. Cultural differences in metaphors, such as how different languages conceptualize time spatially, reveal that assumed universal metaphors are often culturally specific. Good metaphors don't just explain ideas but transform how minds engage with concepts, opening new ways of thinking rather than simply mapping complex unknowns to complex knowns.
